Talk outline: Sampling Design for Spatial Cluster Randomized Trials Under Heterogeneous Incidence

About 20 minutes of content at the SUDDEN project meeting, Thursday 2026-10-29 (a one-hour meeting with about 40 minutes of open discussion; questions may come during the talk, so ±a few minutes is fine). Audience: the clinicians and epidemiologists of the larger SUD study. Goal: share the current state of the project and collect feedback we have not thought of. Draft 3 (2026-10-28), built from the V5-revised CTJ manuscript (commit 00270ae plus the 2026-10-28 declarations fix), its SI, Chapter 3 and the methods-extension results. Each slide is tagged prelim (carries over to prelim Part II), technical (needs a more technical version for biostatisticians) or talk-only.

The deck is sudden_talk_2026-10-29.qmd (rendered to sudden_talk_2026-10-29.html; press S for the speaker view with the read-aloud script, one sentence per bullet). The slide entries below are generated from the deck by python3 presentation/tools/outline_from_deck.py; outline.html is the visual version (python3 presentation/tools/build_outline_html.py). Files are listed in README.md.

Author decisions shaping Draft 3 (2026-10-28; reasons in DECISIONS.md)

  • Title is the manuscript title; only Andrew on the title slide; Dr. Lin (advisor), Dr. Simpson and Ashkan Habib (collaborators) credited on the thank-you slide, with UNC IRB protocol 14-2036 and "manuscript in preparation for Clinical Trials".
  • Background covers SUD's relevance, Dr. Simpson's Lenoir County pilot idea and its progression to a statewide trial, and how the 100 counties became 58 college service areas. Flowcharts show SUD case identification and the application study pipeline.
  • The model slide shows the full equation with every term defined, read in words, and explains how each trial is simulated and estimated.
  • Take-home: Incidence-Guided Saturation is a reasonable middle ground with limited downside across both spillover regimes; the final choice still depends on the expected spillover and participation (refines the no-single-recommended-design rule).
  • Saturation Quadrants, the targeting slide and the questions for the group are backup only; the questions are raised as needed, some to Dr. Simpson.
  • Regime names stay "controls only" and "both arms", glossed as untreated colleges gain / every college gains.
  • Script is read aloud, one sentence per bullet.
  • An outline (agenda) slide after the title lists the five sections.
  • Case identification follows Gan et al.'s documented steps (age, place, manner, cancer); the statewide data's additional exclusion rules are mentioned generically, to clarify verbally. The pilot's trainees (students and staff in workforce-development and disaster-response programs, possibly EMS and healthcare trainees) and its process measures (taking medicine, timely clinic visits) are flagged for Dr. Simpson to confirm.

Draft 1 (2026-10-25, in git history) set the order (motivation, models, designs, grid, NC application, conclusions), most claim titles, the plain regime names, the audience questions and most backup topics. Kept from its notes: ask how many colleges will join; guidance costs no accuracy, a defensible equity choice; the colleges-needed counts use a test with 5% size. 3. Sudden unexpected death takes a large and uneven toll on working-age adults

0.75 minprelim
none
Slide text
Nationally Sudden unexpected death (SUD): an unexpected natural death outside the hospital in a working-age adult About 49 per 100,000 men and 22 per 100,000 women aged 20–64 each year (US estimate from SUDDEN adjudication in Wake County) About 2 million years of life lost, 10% of all-cause years of life lost at these ages, and about $51 billion in lifetime productivity loss Mirzaei et al., Medical Care 2019; Gan …
Notes
Sudden unexpected death is why this project exists, an unexpected natural death outside the hospital in a working-age adult. Dr. Simpson's group estimated about 49 per 100,000 men and 22 per 100,000 women aged 20 to 64 die this way each year, about two million years of life lost.

4. Dr. Simpson's Lenoir County pilot is the starting point for a statewide trial

1.5 minprelim
none
Slide text
SUD as a social problem SUDDEN findings show sudden death tracks access to care, income and rurality, so prevention has to reach communities, not only hospitals → Lenoir County pilot idea Teach SUD prevention through Lenoir Community College's workforce-development and disaster-response training (Lenoir, Greene and Jones counties), where Dr. Simpson notes SUD rates spike after flooding → Trainees (to confirm) …
Notes
SUDDEN showed that sudden death tracks access to care, income and rurality, so prevention has to reach communities, not only hospitals. Dr. Simpson's pilot idea is to teach SUD prevention through Lenoir Community College's workforce-development and disaster-response training, which serves Lenoir, Greene and Jones counties.

5. When a program reaches neighbors, a simple comparison can miss its effect

0.75 minprelim
none
Slide text
Bed nets, northern Ghana Children living near households with insecticide-treated bed nets had lower mortality, even when their own household had none. School deworming, western Kenya Untreated children attending schools near treated schools had fewer worm infections. Spillover means that treating one group changes outcomes in the groups next to it A trial that compares treated with untreated clusters assumes …
Notes
Two classic examples show why geography matters. In northern Ghana, children living near households with treated bed nets had lower mortality, even without a net of their own.

6. Analysis methods exist, but guidance on which clusters to treat is thin

0.5 mintechnical
none
Slide text
After the trial (analysis) Spatial models separate a program's direct effect from the effect of treated neighbors They need a trial designed to give them that contrast Before the trial (design) Which clusters should be treated? Options serve different goals (balance a covariate, vary the treated share by region, keep treated clusters apart) Few studies compare them under spillover and uneven incidence together …
Notes
Statisticians have good tools for analyzing spillover after a trial, but only if the design gave them enough contrast to work with, and that is decided when we choose which clusters to treat. Several allocation ideas exist, and few studies compare them when spillover and uneven incidence occur together.

2. Methods

8. Spillover can reach only the untreated colleges, or every college

1 minprelim
none
Slide text
Spillover to controls only untreated colleges gain Spillover to both arms treated and untreated colleges gain Treated college Control college Gains from treated neighbors (more treated neighbors, larger gain) Controls only is classic contamination, in which untreated colleges learn from treated neighbors Both arms means treated colleges also gain from treated neighbors, for example through shared trainings Which …
Notes
This is the most important idea in the talk. Spillover can work in two ways.

9. One outcome model links treatment, spillover and neighbors

1 minprelim
none
Slide text
$$ Y = (I - \rho W)^{-1}\left[\,\tau Z + S(Z) + \beta X + \epsilon\,\right], \qquad \epsilon \sim N(0, I) $$ Spillover to both arms $S(Z) = \gamma\, WZ$ Spillover to controls only $S(Z) = \gamma\,(1 - Z) \circ WZ$ $Y$ Outcome of each cluster (in the application, a college's mean education score) $Z$ Treatment indicator, 1 if the cluster is treated and 0 if control $W$ Neighbor matrix. Under queen contiguity two …
Notes
You don't need the algebra, since every symbol is defined below, so I'll say it in words. A college's score Y is the direct effect of its own treatment, tau times Z, plus spillover from treated neighbors, S of Z, plus a possible effect of incidence, beta times X, plus noise.

10. We judge each design by its average error, its intervals and its worst allocations

0.75 minprelim
none
Slide text
We estimate the program's effect $\tau$ with a spatial model that allows for spillover (a spatial lag model fitted by maximum likelihood, including the true spillover term), and repeat the trial thousands of times in simulation. Mean squared error (MSE) The average of $(\hat\tau - \tau)^2$ over simulated trials. It combines bias and imprecision. Lower is better. Coverage The share of 95% confidence intervals that …
Notes
We judge each design three ways. We simulate the trial thousands of times and estimate the effect each time with a spatial model that includes the spillover.

23. A one-SD college effect is a modest effect for each trained professional

0.75 minprelim
none
Slide text
A college score averages $m$ professionals. With intraclass correlation ICC (share of score variance between colleges), the college-level noise SD ($\epsilon$), in individual SD units, is $$\sigma_c = \sqrt{\text{ICC} + (1 - \text{ICC})/m}$$ so a college effect of $\tau$ SDs is an individual effect of $d = \tau\,\sigma_c$. With 25 professionals per college and ICC = 0.05 , $\sigma_c \approx 0.30$, so a one-SD …
Notes
What does one college-level standard deviation mean in practice? The college score averages the professionals assessed there, and averaging reduces noise.

5. Discussion

24. Incidence-Guided Saturation was a reasonable middle ground with limited downside

1 minprelim
none
Slide text
Incidence-Guided Saturation gained the most under controls-only spillover, at a small cost under both arms Spillover to controls only (untreated colleges gain) Lowest or near-lowest error with all colleges taking part (21–30% below SRS in NC, 37% on the grid), a lower risk of an unlucky allocation, and the most treatment in the highest-rate region (a small shift on the NC map, where regions are similar). Even …
Notes
The goal is a design that does reasonably well whichever kind of spillover is true, with limited downside. Incidence-Guided Saturation gained the most when spillover reaches untreated colleges, at a small cost when it reaches everyone, while Balanced Quartiles stayed close to random sampling in both.

A few limits. Our analysis assumed we know how spillover works, and if the analysis ignores spillover, every design underestimates the effect.

Rook neighbors share an edge only. Under controls only …

Use when asked about the neighbor definition or why strict alternation fails. In NC, rook and queen at matched settings gave the same broad conclusions. Figure: SI rook comparison with SRS (fig_vs_srs_by_regime_rook).

technical
none

Notes
Use when asked "what if we don't know the spillover form?" We did not study a spillover term of the wrong form (wrong network or distance decay); that is listed as future work. Source: CTJ Results; Chapter 3 non-oracle sensitivity.

Use when asked why the intervals are not the usual Wald intervals. Maximum likelihood variance divides by N and the normal reference ignores estimated parameters, so with 58 or fewer clusters Wald intervals are too narrow. Bootstrap and profile-likelihood intervals did not meet the 94–96% rule. Sources: results/grid_tdf_2026-10/interval_comparison.csv; Chapter 3 tab:nc-calibration.

B16. Guidance gains grow with how much regions differ

technical
Slide text
Each point is one simulated grid incidence surface, plotting the spread of the regions' mean incidence ranks against the extra treated share of incidence from incidence guidance over random-order saturation. NC's four planning years (open triangles) sit at the low-spread end and below the grid trend.
Notes
Use when asked "why does guidance barely change targeting in NC?" On the grid the gain was 2.1–3.1 percentage points, correlation with spread 0.84–0.99. NC regions' mean ranks lie between 24 and 34 of 58 in every year. Source: Chapter 3 Appendix A9 (fig:spread-gain).
